title: CBI: three distinct views of exhaustion (descriptive)

qcReview.basis: Checked against the official NFA English CBI scale sheet and current NFA reuse notice. Score-only adult draft: three separate dimensions, no total, thresholds, norms, diagnosis, or performance inference. Human occupational-health and final rights sign-off remain pending.

interpretations.headline: Start with the pattern, not a label
interpretations.summary: This score is the mean of six questions about prolonged physical and psychological fatigue or exhaustion. A higher value means that these experiences were reported more often; it does not identify their cause. Use this result to name the pattern you have noticed and to decide what context needs a closer look, including recovery, health, family demands, and work. It is not a diagnosis and it should not be read as a measure of resilience or personal worth.

guidance.text: Look back over a recent ordinary week and note when your energy dropped, what happened just before it, and what helped it recover.
If exhaustion is persistent, worsening, or interfering with daily life, discuss the broader picture with an appropriate health or workplace support; this score alone cannot explain it.

interpretations.headline: Ask what work is contributing
interpretations.summary: This score is the mean of seven questions about exhaustion that you attribute to work. The final question about having energy for family and friends is reverse-scored, as specified by the original CBI. A higher value describes a stronger work-related exhaustion pattern; it does not show that you are performing poorly or prove that one particular job condition caused it. Its most useful role is to open a concrete conversation about work design, demands, resources, and recovery.

guidance.text: Choose one recent workday and identify the task, deadline, interruption, or staffing condition that consumed the most energy.
Turn that example into one workable request, such as clarifying priorities, adjusting a deadline, protecting a break, or adding a resource.

interpretations.headline: Use only when people-facing work fits your role
interpretations.summary: This score is the mean of six questions about exhaustion attributed to working with clients. In the official CBI, “clients” may include patients, social-service recipients, older citizens, or inmates. The score is meaningful only when that kind of people-facing work is part of your role and the wording fits your setting. A higher value is a prompt to examine the demands and support surrounding those interactions, not a judgment of your attitude, empathy, or professional quality.

guidance.text: Identify one type of interaction that is especially draining and separate what belongs to the interaction itself from workload, role boundaries, or missing support.
Consider one relevant support around that work, such as supervision, peer consultation, safer boundaries, debriefing, or a change in service arrangements.

limitations: The CBI defines three distinct scales. This report does not create or imply an overall burnout total.
Personal burnout describes general exhaustion; work-related and client-related scores describe exhaustion attributed by the respondent to those contexts. The scores do not establish causation.
Client-related burnout should be used only when client-facing work applies and the canonical English referent is appropriate. Any teacher/student adaptation requires a separately governed version.
No diagnostic cutoff, severity band, norm, percentile, or score-derived label is applied. The three means are descriptive 0–100 scores.
The official non-response rules are preserved: personal and client-related scores require at least three answered items, and work-related burnout requires at least four.

NFA permits commercial and non-commercial use provided the required source is clearly cited: Borritz M et al., Burnout among employees in human service work: design and baseline findings of the PUMA study, Scandinavian Journal of Public Health (2006), 34, 49–58.
report.disclaimer: These self-reported CBI scores are descriptive. They are not a medical diagnosis, a fitness-for-work decision, or a measure of employee performance.
